title: Krishna's measured yoga
hookLine: a calendar with every square filled, and Krishna's verse about food, sleep and work as yoga
carry: work is yoga, and yoga is measured
tomorrow: a teacher's send-off says give with fear. why fear?

cards: The calendar is taped to the bedroom wall, and it's beautiful. Green squares for the food pantry, every Saturday. Blue for tutoring, every weeknight.
Orange for early errands for the neighbor down the hall. Not one white square left. Its maker steps back, proud, and then a small cold thought arrives.
What happens on the week of exams? The week of the flu? Krishna has an answer for that wall, and he gives it in the middle of a lesson on meditation, of all places.

teach.h: NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE.
teach.b: In chapter six of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to sit and steady the mind. Then he turns practical. Yoga, he says, isn't for the one who eats too much, or for the one who doesn't eat at all.
It isn't for the one who sleeps too much, or the one who's always awake.
Then the key line, in paraphrase: for the one who is measured in eating and resting, measured in effort at work, measured in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the end of sorrow.
The Sanskrit for measured is yukta: fitted, joined, in proportion. Look at what sits in the middle of that list. Effort in actions.

teach.h: KARMA YOGA: WORK AS A PATH TO GOD.
teach.b: That's karma yoga, one of the Gita's great teachings: work itself can be a path to God, as much a practice as sitting still. And a practice isn't a punishment.
In chapter seventeen Krishna goes further: those who torment the body with harsh austerities, he says, torment me too, the one who dwells within it.
Many teachers read that as a root of Hindu balance: the body is a home of the divine, not an enemy to beat.

teach.h: WORK IS YOGA. YOGA IS MEASURED.
teach.b: So a year of service, if it's karma yoga, gets the care of a vow: an amount that can be kept on a bad week, and rest that's planned, not stolen. This isn't a lower bar.
The measured person isn't doing less of what matters. They're doing it as yoga, so it's still being done when the year runs out.

how: Hindu teachers who draw on Gita 6.16–17 and 17.5–6 counsel balance in food, sleep and work, and warn against punishing the body, so that practice and service can be steady over a lifetime rather than intense for a season.

games.q: your friends want to visit a lonely neighbor. someone proposes every single day, starting tomorrow. by Gita chapter six, what's the better plan?
o: every day. real care means no days off.
a pace the group can keep, with rest planned in.
wait until summer, when everyone is free.
games.why: Krishna lists effort at work beside food and sleep: karma yoga, kept in measure, ends sorrow instead of making more. a visit that lasts all year beats one that burns out in a week.

practice: On paper or in a note, write one kind thing you already do that's small enough to keep up on your most tired week. Under it, write when you'll rest from it.
Then breathe at an easy pace, not long, not short, with the page in front of you.

wordCard.voice: Karma: action, offered as yoga and kept in measure like food and sleep, so a year of service is still going at its end.

orig.note: Sanskrit yukta, joined or fitted; in Gita chapter six, measured, in proportion.

carryVoice: Keep this: work is yoga, and yoga is measured. Day three of the capstone, done.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 6.16–17 (yoga is not for one who eats or sleeps too much or too little; for the one measured in food, recreation, effort in actions, sleep and waking, yoga destroys sorrow)
Bhagavad Gita 17.5–6 (those who perform harsh austerities not enjoined by scripture, torturing the elements of the body and me who dwells within the body)
